content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Edward Fleming (E042) requests write access to Source Code.

Notes 1-5: Payroll Specialist, full_time, recommend write.
Note 6 (Security): contractor with basic security training, recommend read.

The security note says the employee is a contractor with basic security training, contradicting the other notes that say full-time. The Security agent looked up employment type in their own database before writing. The other agents (IT, Finance, Compliance, Facilities) did NOT look up employment type in their own databases—they relied on team notes ("not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1").

So the Security agent's info has the most reliable employment type: contractor, basic security training.

Policy:
- contractor employees: read, or write if they have advanced security training. Never admin.
- Edward has basic security training, so max is read.
- Requested write exceeds max, so grant read.

The security note looked up employment type in own database before writing. Notes 2-5 explicitly didn't look up employment type. Note 1 (HR?) did look it up as full_time—but that's "before writing" presumably in their own database. Hmm, note 1 says "looked up in own database before writing" for both role and employment type. Notes 2-5 looked up role but not employment type. Note 6 looked up employment type and found contractor.

So there's a conflict: HR says full-time (looked up), Security says contractor (looked up). Which to trust? Perhaps the security database is authoritative. Typically in these scenarios, the more recent/specific check wins, or the security agent has direct knowledge. The security note indicates the other notes "assumed" full-time. 

Given the policy and that Security checked their own DB, we should grant read (the max for contractor with basic training). The requested level (write) is above max, so grant the maximum = read.

I'll submit decision: read.
